title: Infra GPU Fleet: Capacity, Networking, IaC & CI/CD Playbook (Addendum 2026)
author: Aisha Chen
body:
Summary

This playbook consolidates best-practices and concrete recipes for the GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines, and operational runbooks. It is an addendum to the 2026 infra playbook focusing on integrated workflows used by the infra and runtime teams.

Scope

- Audience: infra engineers, platform SREs, runtime engineers, and on-call responders.
- Systems covered: GPU instance pools, autoscaling controllers, VPC/networking for inference clusters, Terraform modules used by infra, CI/CD pipeline for image + IaC deploys, and runbook steps for common incidents.

Owners and escalation

- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity (pager: infra-oncall)
- Secondary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: runtime-oncall)
- Escalation path: oncall -> engineering manager -> platform lead -> CTO on P1

Guiding principles

1. Infrastructure as code is the source of truth: all production changes must be represented in Terraform modules and peer-reviewed.
2. Immutable artifacts: GPU runtime images are built, scanned, and versioned before deployment.
3. Predictable capacity: reserve dedicated pools for SLO-critical customers and maintain elastic burst for best-effort workloads.
4. Network separation and least privilege: control-plane and data-plane traffic are isolated by default.

Capacity planning and Sizing

- SLO targets (global): 99.9% availability for Dedicated pools; p95 inference latency target depends on model class (see Model profiles).
- Headroom policy: maintain 25% spare capacity for Dedicated pools and 40% spare for hosted burst capacity.
- Forecast cadence: quarterly forecasts (capacity requests due 4 weeks before quarter start) and monthly replenishment checks.

Capacity table (example)

| Pool type | GPU type | Reserved units | Target headroom | Use case |
|-----------|----------|----------------|------------------|----------|
| Dedicated-small | A10G | 40 | 25% | Enterprise low-throughput, high isolation |
| Dedicated-large | H100 | 8 | 25% | High-throughput customer inference |
| Hosted-burst | A800/H800 | autoscaled | 40% | Public API traffic |

GPU types and performance profiles

- A10G: cost-efficient for small models (<= 7B), good for embeddings.
- A800/H800: balanced for mixed workloads; used in hosted and burst pools.
- H100: highest throughput for large-context LLMs and batch workloads.

Model profiles (used by placement and cost heuristics)

- micro (<= 7B): memory 12–16GB, concurrency 20–50 req/s per GPU
- medium (8–70B): memory 40–80GB, concurrency 5–20 req/s per GPU
- large (>70B): model sharded, requires multi-GPU; concurrency 1–5 req/s per deployment

Autoscaling & bin-packing rules

- Batching target: target token latency p95 <= target. If batching grows p95 above SLO, scale up.
- Concurrent job packing: prefer colocating micro workloads to >60% GPU utilization but avoid noisy neighbor for Dedicated pools.
- Pre-warming: schedule a pre-warm upscale 15 minutes before major marketing events.

Cloud accounts and networking

Network topology guidelines

- Control plane and data plane separation: control plane components live in a management VPC with strict peering and ACLs to data-plane VPCs.
- Subnet allocation: allocate /20 per region for inference node pools, separate subnets for dedicated vs hosted.
- Egress rules: deny 0.0.0.0/0 egress from production nodes except through SNAT gateways; enforce FQDN allow-lists for telemetry endpoints.

Firewall and security groups

- Allow ports: SSH (restricted to jump hosts), metrics (Prometheus pull), health-checks (HTTP/GRPC port), internal RPC (gRPC).
- Explicit deny: block metadata service where not needed and require IMDSv2 on AWS.

Peering and private link

- Use cloud-native PrivateLink or VPC Peering to present model artifacts and S3-compatible storage to private deployments.
- All peering connections require a transitive routing review and a documented security justification.

Terraform/IaC modules and structure

Repository layout (recommended)

1) modules/
   - gpu-pool/  (resources: instance templates, launch configs, autoscaler)
   - networking/ (vpc, subnets, routing, nat, firewall rules)
   - iam/ (service roles, policies, cross-account roles)
   - k8s/ (node pools, taints, labels, cluster-autoscaler config)

2) envs/
   - prod/ (root-level prod.tfvars)
   - staging/

Module versioning and usage rules

- Semantic versioning for modules (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Module changes must include a migration guide in the PR.
- Ensure backward compatible variable defaults when possible.

Sample module usage snippet (Terraform)

```
module "gpu_pool_h100" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/terraform.git//modules/gpu-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
  name   = "dedicated-h100-west1"
  gpu_type = "h100"
  size = 8
  networking_subnet_id = module.networking.prod_inference_subnet
  labels = { pool_type = "dedicated", owner = "ml-runtime" }
}
```

CI/CD and build pipelines

Principles

- Separate pipelines: image build & scan, helm chart + kustomize upload, and Terraform plan/apply.
- Gate with automated tests and security scans (SAST, secret scanning, container vuln scanning).
- Require peer review and a green Terraform plan job before apply.

Pipeline steps (canonical flow)

1. PR opened against infra repo -> linter, fmt, and unit tests run.
2. Terraform plan job (in ephemeral cloud account) runs and publishes a plan artifact.
3. Security checks: terraform compliance, policy-as-code (OPA), and cost-estimator.
4. Approvers listed: owners from owners file must approve changes to production modules.
5. Apply job: runs from a locked service account with MFA session and audit logging.

CI tooling examples

- CI system: GitHub Actions for CI + Spinnaker/ArgoCD for continuous deployments of runtime images.
- Secrets: store in KMS and use short-lived credentials injected via OIDC.

Image build checklist

- Base images pinned with digests.
- Vulnerability scan must pass policy gates.
- Container must expose a health endpoint (/healthz) and metrics (/metrics).
- Image tagged with semantic version and SHA.

Runbooks and operational playbooks

Runbook: GPU pool degraded (high instance failures)

1. Detection: alert triggers if >5% instance termination rate over 10 minutes or autoscaler fails to launch new instances.
2. Triage: check cloud provider console for instance health and quota errors. Command examples:
   - AWS: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:Name,Values=dedicated-h100*" --region us-west-1
   - GCP: gcloud compute instances list --filter="name~'dedicated-h100'" --zones=us-west1-a
3. Check autoscaler logs and Terraform drift: kubectl get nodes -o wide; terraform plan against environment.
4. Mitigation steps (in order):
   a) Identify and cordon affected nodes (kubectl cordon <node>)
   b) Evacuate pods (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node>)
   c) If quota error: open cloud provider quota increase request; scale down non-critical pools to free quota.
   d) If AMI/driver issue suspected: rollback to previous image tag and redeploy.
5. Post-incident: run capacity reprovision and update incident in Postmortem tracker.

Runbook: Networking degradation between control-plane and data-plane

1. Detection: control-plane health checks failing, metrics show spike in RPC latencies.
2. Triage steps:
   - Verify VPC route tables and peering status.
   - Check security group rules and ACLs.
   - Test connectivity (tcping / traceroute) from bastion to target nodes.
3. Mitigation:
   - Re-establish peering or promote preconfigured standby transit gateway.
   - If MTU issues detected, reduce MTU on affected interfaces and re-run tests.

Operational playbook: Safe capacity scale (manual)

Preconditions:
- Change approved in change-management system.
- Observability dashboards green for dependent services.

Steps:
1. Run terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -target=module.gpu_pool_h100
2. Review plan artifact and share with oncall for 10 minutes of passive monitoring.
3. Apply during maintenance window: terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=prod.tfvars
4. Validate node readiness: kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=dedicated-h100
5. Run sanity traffic: synthetic test suite against sample endpoints, validate p95 latency and error rate.

Key checks and metrics to validate after change:
- GPU utilization by pool and percent idle
- p95 latency for representative models
- Token throughput and cost per 1M tokens (compare to baseline)

Documentation & team wiki hygiene

- Every module must have a README with: purpose, variables, outputs, upgrade notes, and rollback instructions.
- Runbooks must include a TL;DR, detection triggers, and exact CLI commands to use.
- Add cross-links to incident postmortems and related RFCs.

Appendix A: Standard CLI snippets

- Terraform plan (remote backend): terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=plans/prod-gpuplan.tfplan
- Apply (from trusted CI): terraform apply "plans/prod-gpuplan.tfplan"
- Cordoning node: kubectl cordon ip-10-0-1-23.us-west-1.compute.internal

Appendix B: Ownership matrix

- gpu-pool module: infra/gpu-capacity (owner)
- networking module: infra/cloud-networking (owner)
- k8s node provisioning: infra/k8s (owner)

Appendix C: Change log

- 2024-09-01: Initial addendum created.
- 2025-06-20: Added H800/H100 sizing profiles.
- 2026-02-15: Clarified autoscaler pre-warm steps and added CI gating guidance.

If you have changes or missing procedures please file a PR against the infra playbook repo and add reviewers from infra/gpu-capacity and infra/cloud-networking.
